posts.title: Alt text: describe the picture in one sentence
posts.hook: Alt text: describe the picture in one sentence. Five quick rules for the pictures on your website.
posts.facebook:
Alt text: describe the picture in one sentence. Five quick rules for the pictures on your website.
See how we build websites everyone can use: https://ka-performancefl.com/services/web-design/?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=2026-10-17

1. What it's for. A screen reader reads alt text aloud to someone who can't see the picture, and the browser shows it when the picture doesn't load.
2. One sentence. Say who or what is in it, and what's happening. The page around it tells the story.
3. What not to write. Skip "image of" (the screen reader already says it's an image), file names like IMG_2041.jpg, and paragraphs.
4. When to leave it empty. If a picture is only decoration, or only repeats the words right next to it, use an empty alt: alt="". Don't delete the alt entirely.
5. Where to type it. Click the picture in your site editor, open its settings, and find the box called Alt text or Alternative text.

The prompt: Copy this prompt. It asks for notes, not a new version. A printed sheet with the full prompt: Proofread the paragraph below from my small business website. Do not rewrite it. Don't suggest new wording for style, tone or flow, and don't give me a revised version. It's in my voice and I want to keep it that way. Only list: 1. Errors: spelling, grammar and punctuation. Quote the exact words and give the smallest fix. 2. Unclear sentences: quote the sentence and say in a few words what a reader might misread. Don't rewrite it. 3. Facts to check: every date, number, price, time or claim I should confirm before this goes live. If a section has nothing, say "None." Keep it short. Paragraph: [paste your paragraph]. A sticky note: Screenshot this. Change nothing but the paragraph.

We tried it: A real run, on a made-up dog groomer. Tagged Fictional business, made up for this example. The printed draft: We opened Scruff & Suds in 2014, which means we've been washing muddy dogs for over fifteen years now. Every groom starts with a warm bath, a nail trim and a ear check, and we never rush a nervous pup. If your dog doesn't like the dryer, tell us and we'll towel dry them instead, it takes longer but their worth it. Walk-ins are welcome Tuesday through Saturday, 8 to 5, and a full groom for a small dog is $45. Pick up is by 4 so we can clean up before closing. A sticky note from us: We wrote it with a few mistakes on purpose. Let's see what it finds.

What came back, 1 of 3: Errors, with the smallest fix. The draft with five numbered marks and five yellow sticky notes quoting the AI model word for word: 1. "a ear check": change to "an ear check". 2. "their worth it": change to "they're worth it". 3. "towel dry them instead, it takes longer": two full sentences are joined with only a comma. Change the comma to a semicolon or a period. 4. "Pick up is by 4": used as a noun, it's one word. Change to "Pickup". 5, optional: "towel dry" (optional): used as a verb, it's usually hyphenated, "towel-dry". Tagged Checked by an AI model, word for word, and Fictional business.

What came back, 2 of 3: Unclear sentences, and what a reader might misread. Two sentences underlined on the draft and two mint sticky notes, word for word: A. "Pick up is by 4 so we can clean up before closing." A reader might think you pick dogs up, like a pickup service, not that owners must collect them by 4. B. "Walk-ins are welcome Tuesday through Saturday, 8 to 5..." It isn't clear whether these are your business hours or only walk-in hours. Pickup is by 4, so a reader may wonder whether a walk-in after about 3 can still be groomed. No rewrite. It says what's unclear and leaves the wording to you.

What came back, 3 of 3: Facts only you can check. Coral notes, word for word: "in 2014" and "over fifteen years" don't agree. 2014 to 2026 is 12 years. Confirm which one is right. And: "we never rush a nervous pup": make sure your staff can back up this promise. A yellow list of the rest: Every groom includes a warm bath, a nail trim and an ear check. Towel drying is offered instead of the dryer. The walk-in days, Tuesday through Saturday. The hours, 8 to 5 (AM to PM is implied). The $45 price for a full groom on a small dog, and what counts as "small." The pickup deadline of 4.

Your part: Then you make the fixes, in your words. 1. Did it rewrite anything? Ours didn't: no new version, no style notes, only the smallest fixes. 2. Fix the errors yourself, one at a time, so every sentence stays yours. 3. Answer what only you know: the year, the hours, the price, the promise. The draft with the owner's pencil fixes, a drawn example: over fifteen years crossed out for twelve years, a ear for an ear, instead, it for instead. Local search, done properly: https://ka-performancefl.com/services/seo-ai-search/?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=2026-10-19-2

1. Reply in public. Thank them by name and mention what they mentioned. The next customer reads your reply too.

5. Ask the next happy customer. Share your Google review link or QR code. Offer nothing in return: Google doesn't allow incentives for reviews.

A good Google review can do more work after you say thanks. Five things to do with it:

1. Reply in public. Thank them by name and mention what they mentioned. The next customer reads your reply too, so it is part of your first impression.

2. Answer the question it raised, on your site. When a review says "I didn't know you did that," other people didn't know either. Put the answer on the page where they look first.

3. Quote it on your site. Ask first. Then use their words exactly, with their permission, on the page the review is about.

4. Fix what it flagged. A fair complaint is free advice. Fix it, then say so in your reply, where the next customer will see it.

5. Ask the next happy customer. Google gives every business profile a review link and a QR code. Share it when someone says thanks in person, and offer nothing in return: Google doesn't allow incentives for reviews.

The examples in this document use a fictional diner.

What we check before a website goes live, shown on a site we built and already launched: Thrillers Mobile VR (thrillersvr.com).

Seven checks, captured on the live site on Sept 30:

1. Tab through it. Every stop on the home page, in order, with a focus ring you can see. Thrillers has 26, and the first one is "Skip to content."

2. The 10-second phone test. On the first phone screen, with no scrolling, a new visitor can say what the business is and where it is.

3. Contrast. Text colors measured against WCAG, not eyeballed. The minimum is 4.5:1; the lowest pair on Thrillers is 7.55:1.

4. Every link returns 200. Every page on the site, and every link on each page. Six pages, six 200s.

5. The form sends. Labels, required marks, and an error that says what to fix, then one test send before launch. For this document we only captured the field states; nothing was sent through the client's form.

6. The 404 page. A wrong address should return a real 404 status and give people a way back, not a blank page.

7. Speed on a phone. More on that soon.

More quick fixes on our YouTube channel: https://www.youtube.com/@KAPerformancefl
